9th Street, Eastleigh · Kamukunji Sub-County · Nairobi City County · collapse of 23 Oct 2026

Eastleigh Collapse GIS Atlas

Open geospatial data around the collapsed 18-storey building, used to test the foundation explanation, map exposure of neighbours, check emergency access and screen the district for similar high-rise stock. The plot is not yet confirmed: the site is taken as the Ninth Street / 2nd Avenue Eastleigh junction, ±100 m.

PLATE A

Site context

  • The block is dense: footprints sit edge to edge, with storey-tagged neighbours of 9 to 13 floors within 70 m.
  • Ninth Street is a narrow residential street; the building fronts a dense grid of similar plots.
Context only: confirm the exact plot (LR number or GPS) before drawing site-specific conclusions.

Data: Esri World Imagery (Esri, Maxar, Earthstar Geographics); OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL); site location from press reports. Credit: Gava Charles

PLATE B

Terrain and hydrology

  • Site at about 1,647 m, on the interfluve between the Mathare and Nairobi river valleys.
  • Nearest watercourse: Mathare River, 1,287 m away and about 27 m lower. Terrain slope about 3°.
  • No floodplain, steep slope or mapped drain at the site.
Terrain gives no foundation trigger. A footing failure would need a soil cause (black-cotton clay, weathered tuff, groundwater, adjacent excavation), which only a site investigation can show.

Data: AWS Terrain Tiles (Tilezen; SRTM-derived in Kenya, ~30 m, ±5 m); OpenStreetMap waterways. Credit: Gava Charles

PLATE B2

Antecedent rainfall

  • 4 mm in the 7 days before the collapse and 45 mm in 30 days, at the onset of the short rains.
  • The wettest day was 10 Oct with 12 mm.
No unusual rainfall: wet ground is unlikely to have triggered the collapse.

Data: Open-Meteo daily precipitation (weather-model / reanalysis blend, ~11 km grid; not a rain gauge). Credit: Gava Charles

PLATE C

Exposure of neighbours

  • 34 footprints within 55 m (one building height), 56 more within 110 m.
  • The video shows a near-vertical, in-footprint collapse, so impact damage should concentrate on the immediately adjoining buildings.
  • Dust ran down the street canyons; the corridors mark where people were exposed.
Inspect the adjoining buildings before reoccupation, especially any built by the same developer or contractor.

Data: Esri World Imagery; OpenStreetMap contributors; height ~55 m from press reports. Credit: Gava Charles

PLATE D

Emergency access

  • Only two fire stations are mapped: Nairobi Fire Station about 4.3 km by road and Kangundo Road about 7.0 km.
  • Several hospitals lie within about 1 km.
  • The last few hundred metres are residential and service streets, which crowds and parked vehicles block easily. Reports describe exactly that.
Times are free-flow estimates; real response in Eastleigh is much slower.

Data: Esri Light Gray Canvas; OpenStreetMap roads and facilities; routing with networkx (this analysis). Credit: Gava Charles

PLATE E

High-rise screening

  • 314 buildings of 8 or more storeys are mapped within 2 km, clustered through Eastleigh.
  • Only 318 of 17,596 footprints carry storey tags, so the true count is higher.
A proper screen would add satellite-derived heights and county permits to rank buildings for inspection.

Data: Esri Light Gray Canvas; OpenStreetMap contributors. Credit: Gava Charles
